problems.description: Discrepancy with mechanical measurement: convention score 0.69 / 13 violations, but every listed violation (app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py — PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE) references files NOT in this diff. Both files in this commit (task_api.py, test_task_api.py) are convention-clean, so the commit's own code rates well above 0.69.

`app.run(debug=True)` in the __main__ block hardcodes debug mode rather than deriving it from an env var; harmless here but a pattern that could leak debug introspection if copied into later sessions.
`status` accepts any non-empty string with no enum/state validation, so invalid task states can be persisted; fine for greenfield but may need a constraint as the story grows.
Single-file module with no blueprint/package split; appropriate for the current scope, but later sessions that add notification/celery features may need restructuring.

strengths: Idiomatic Flask app-factory pattern with per-request sqlite3 connection via `g` and teardown handling — testable and correct
All SQL is parameterized (injection-safe)
136-line test suite covering success and error paths (missing/blank/non-string title, 404, ordering, partial updates)
UTC ISO timestamps, graceful JSON error handlers, defensive input validation
commit_reviews.summary: Clean greenfield Flask/SQLite task API with idiomatic patterns and thorough tests; the low 0.69 convention score is driven entirely by files outside this commit, so it should not be attributed to this change.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-me' when the env var is unset, making all JWTs forgeable in any environment that forgets to configure it; safer to fail fast when SECRET_KEY is absent.
Password validation only checks non-empty, so whitespace-only passwords are accepted; no minimum length or strength requirement on /auth/register.
No rate limiting or lockout on /auth/login, leaving the endpoint open to brute-force attempts.

require_auth injects the user row as a positional argument into every handler, changing all handler signatures; the codebase already uses flask `g` for the db connection, so storing the user on `g` would be more consistent and avoid signature churn.
The ALTER TABLE migration path adds owner_id without a real enforced FK constraint (SQLite), so referential integrity relies on application logic.
No tests cover the new auth flows (register/login/protected routes, expired/invalid tokens) in this session.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored in plaintext.
All task queries are owner-scoped (WHERE owner_id = ?), preventing cross-user data access (IDOR).
Graceful migration for pre-existing databases without owner_id via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE.
Mirrors existing codebase patterns: nested handlers inside create_app, task_to_dict serializer, consistent JSON error shape, UPPER_CASE module constants.
Stateless JWT with exp and iat claims; token validation re-checks the user still exists.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-structured multi-user JWT auth + ownership-scoping feature that improves the API and follows existing patterns, though the hardcoded default SECRET_KEY is a real security debt — and note the 0.69 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files outside this commit (app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py), not the task_api.py changes, which themselves adhere to conventions.

problems.description: celery_config.py declares module-level settings in lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes). The static analyzer flags these as needing UPPER_CASE, though lowercase is idiomatic Celery config-module style consumed by config_from_object.
Several of the 13 flagged violations appear to be analyzer false positives: conftest.py contains no function or class definitions, yet is flagged for both, and notifications.py defines no classes.
send_notification_email emits the same message via both print() and logger.info(); the print is redundant with structured logging.
conftest.py uses os.environ.setdefault, so an ambient CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER=false in CI would silently disable eager mode and make the suite depend on a live broker.
Notification dispatch is inlined in the PATCH route handler rather than abstracted behind a service/hook; acceptable for a mocked story but couples transport wiring to the route.

strengths: Broker-free testability achieved cleanly: conftest.py sets CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER before any app/celery import, so tests never need Redis.
Legacy-schema migration for the new users.email column mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern in init_db.
Duplicate-notification guard (previous_status check) prevents re-sending on repeated completion updates.
Strong test coverage of new behavior: default email, explicit email, blank-email 400, users-table migration, and notification-trigger path.
Clear module separation (celery_config / notifications / wiring) with docstrings on every new module.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration session that layers Celery notifications onto the task API with migration compatibility, eager-mode testability, and solid tests — the 0.69 convention score is dragged down by analyzer false positives (conftest.py) and lowercase Celery config attrs that are idiomatic rather than violations.

problems.description: get_user_repo()/get_task_repo() closures construct a fresh repository per call rather than caching on Flask's g; harmless here but repeats boilerplate per request and would matter if repos became stateful.

Repositories call self.conn.commit() on every write, hiding transaction boundaries; if a handler ever needs multi-statement atomicity this silently breaks it (fine for the current single-statement routes).
get_by_id and friends return raw sqlite3.Row objects, so the repository layer only isolates SQL, not the storage row type; the route layer still knows it's dealing with sqlite rows.
Type hints are inconsistent — insert(fields: dict) and update(row_id, fields: dict) are annotated but get_by_id/delete/table are not.

strengths: Genuine layering improvement: route handlers no longer touch sqlite3/SQL directly, all access is behind per-table repositories
Reuses the existing per-request g connection pattern instead of introducing new connection management
DRY shared CRUD in BaseRepository with parameterized queries (placeholders preserved, no injection risk)
PascalCase classes and snake_case methods in the touched files match project conventions
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, idiomatic repository-layer refactor that respects the existing Flask g-connection pattern and improves layering, though the 0.69 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py) rather than anything this commit introduced.

problems.description: count_by_owner() runs a COUNT(*) on every paginated page, partially negating the point of keyset pagination (which normally avoids full-scan counting) — O(n) on every page for large owner tables.

GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare JSON array to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope — a breaking contract change for existing clients, shipped without versioning or a compatibility shim.

Ordering semantics changed from 'created_at DESC, id DESC' to 'id DESC' to support the id-based cursor; a silent behavior change for any caller relying on created_at ordering (ties pagination stability to id, which is fine for a cursor but unannounced).

App now hard-requires a reachable Redis at redis://localhost:6379 for flask-limiter storage; if Redis is unavailable the API will error on rate-limited routes (no graceful fallback to in-memory storage).
The JWT is decoded twice per request — once in rate_limit_key() (which runs before require_auth) and again in require_auth — minor duplicate work on every call.

strengths: Correct keyset pagination: fetches limit+1 rows to derive next_cursor and has_more, with the cursor predicate (id < ?) in the repository layer.
Rate limits keyed by authenticated user id with a clean IP fallback for unauthenticated routes, and configured in create_app with an injectable limit making it fully testable.
Thoughtful flask-limiter choices documented inline: application_limits for one shared per-key budget and per-DATABASE key_prefix to isolate counters between app instances.
Pagination covered by real tests using direct DB seeding (seed_tasks) for fast fixtures, following the existing test style (register/login/create_task helpers).
Clear docstrings and comments explaining non-obvious decisions (cursor semantics, pre-auth JWT decode, Redis isolation).
commit_reviews.summary: Well-scoped cross-cutting session adding correct cursor pagination and user-keyed rate limiting that respects the existing repository/app-factory/test patterns, with only minor perf and contract-change nits.

compounding_issues: Binary artifacts (tasks.db, __pycache__/*.pyc) were committed in Session 2 and re-committed with modified contents every session through Session 5, producing noisy unreviewable diffs that persisted to the final tree.
The seed app.py was abandoned dead code from Session 1 onward: never imported, never reused, and never removed even though Sessions 4 and 5 explicitly identified it as such.
Session 5's rate-limit tests couple the suite to a live Redis on localhost:6379 (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI default), so the final test suite silently fails without external infrastructure running.
key_decisions: Greenfield app-factory rewrite (task_api.py with create_app(database=...)) alongside the seed instead of extending app.py — an isolated, testable base every later session depended on.
Per-owner JWT auth in Session 2 (owner_id column, ALTER TABLE migrations, 404-on-cross-user-access) established the multi-tenant security model Session 5's pagination builds on.
Celery notifications with an eager-mode conftest (no broker needed in tests) and transition-only completion trigger (Session 3) — a well-scoped async integration with correct edge-case handling.

Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) in Session 4 — a clean seam that made Session 5's cursor pagination (list_by_owner_page) a near-trivial addition with zero raw SQL in routes.

Session 5 chose Flask-Limiter application_limits over default_limits (one shared per-user budget across all routes), JWT-aware keying, and per-database key_prefix — verified against flask-limiter internals before committing.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The arc runs from a simple CRUD skeleton (16 tests) to a hardened, layered service — security (JWT, per-owner scoping), async integration (Celery notifications with transition-only triggers), a clean repository refactor with zero test breakage, and finally rate limiting plus cursor pagination — ending at 63 passing tests. Effort and cost climbed in lockstep with sophistication, peaking at Session 5 ($1.99, 396s, 53 tool calls) where the agent did genuine library-internals investigation and corrected an initial design mistake (default_limits -> application_limits). The only blemishes are housekeeping debt accumulated early — committed binaries and an abandoned seed file — none of which impaired functionality.
story_review.summary: A textbook logical progression — greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — that compounds into a coherent, well-tested, layered service, marred only by early hygiene choices (committed binaries, dead seed file) that never constrained later sessions.
